title: The dossier closed, the card in your pocket
summary: Light by design and nothing new anywhere. Finish the Expedition dossier down to the run of show and send the invitations, write version two of your protocol card from the pace page rather than from advice, prove the grader account still opens a submit box, and set out the kit for the third crossing.
materials: the Expedition dossier board, markers, and blank cards for the run of show
invitations, and whatever you are sending them by
your protocol card and one fresh index card
the route page and the pace chart from the week 7 crossing
the analog desk clock, and no phone on the desk
laptop with Python and your own usaco.org account
the bug diary and the maker's log

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
Two things get built this week and neither one is a program. One is an event. One is a morning.

Ask: what does a room full of people need in order to understand a thing they were not there for, and what does the version of you sitting down at dawn need from the version of you sitting here now? Those look like two questions. They are the same question twice. Both of them are about writing something down for somebody who will not have you standing beside them.

Imagine: the dossier board finished, so that a person who had never heard of any of this could pick it up, read it, and run the morning without you in the room. That is the real test of a plan, and it is a much harder test than whether you understand it.

Plan: three jobs. Finish the dossier and send the invitations. Write version two of the card and prove the tools. Set out the kit.

And the thing this week says out loud rather than quietly doing. Nothing new is introduced this week, anywhere, in any of the three tracks. No new C++ concept, and none has been introduced since week 9, which is the firewall you closed yourself that week and have kept every day since. The traverse in Think is a crossing of ground you already own. The coins have been on the shelf since week 9. The rehearsal is the ordinary Speak hour wearing better shoes. A week that carries a full contest morning gets no new material stacked on top of it, and that is a decision somebody made on purpose, not a gap somebody left.

Five minutes, Python, and today it is one thing done three times rather than three things done once.

The first forty seconds of every problem on Saturday are the same forty seconds. Type them from memory, closed book, three times, and time yourself on the third one.

File shape, for a contest before the December 2020 one:

    with open("prob.in") as f:
        data = f.read().split()

    with open("prob.out", "w") as f:
        f.write(str(answer) + "\n")

Terminal shape, for the December 2020 contest and everything after it:

    import sys
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    print(answer)

Then the two lines that follow either one and are the same in both: pull the first number out with int(data[0]), and turn the rest into a list of ints. Type those too.

The name prob is a placeholder. On the day it becomes the short name printed on the problem page itself, spelled exactly as the page spells it. You do not remember it, you read it.

No C++ in this drill. Saturday is Python, that was decided in week 1, and the fingers you want warm are the fingers you are going to use.

figure.alt: Temperature through a clear, calm night, drawn as a line that keeps falling past midnight and only turns back up a little after sunrise, once the sun's incoming heat finally outpaces the heat still radiating away. The lowest point of the whole night usually sits just after sunrise, not at midnight the way most people guess.

steps.title: Why the coldest minute of the night is usually the one you get up in
steps.body:
You have been writing one line a day off a min-max thermometer since week 1. Here is something that log knows and almost nobody guesses right.

Ask somebody when the coldest moment of the night is and most people say midnight, or two in the morning, because that is when the night feels most like night. On a clear, calm night the honest answer is usually around sunrise, and often a little after it.

The reason is a running total rather than a clock. All night the ground radiates heat away as infrared, straight up into a sky that gives very little back, and nothing is arriving to replace it, so the total keeps going down. The temperature does not stop falling at some fixed hour. It stops falling at the moment the heat arriving finally catches the heat leaving. The sun does that, but not the instant it appears, because at first light it comes in at a very flat angle and delivers almost nothing. So the losses keep winning for a while after sunrise, and the minimum lands in there.

Three things break the pattern, and they are worth knowing because they are the reason one night proves nothing. Cloud is a blanket that radiates back down, so a cloudy night barely cools. Wind stirs warmer air down from above and stops the cold pooling at the ground. And a weather front moving through can drop the temperature at any hour it likes, and it does not care what time the sun rises.

So here is the week's work, and it is the mirage again wearing a coat. Your instinct says midnight. Your log says something, and it might not agree. Go and read it. On the nights that were still and clear, where did the minimum actually sit? One night is an anecdote. A season of one-line entries is evidence, and you happen to own one.

steps.title: Finish the dossier, and send the invitations
steps.body:
The dossier has been open since week 1 and this week it stops being a pile. A pile is things you know. A dossier is things somebody else could run.

The run of show. Every segment of the morning, in order, with a clock time beside it and a length in minutes. Written as times of day, the way the wall map writes things, because a schedule is a list of places you are travelling to. Leave two gaps in it on purpose, ten minutes each, for the parts that always run long. Something always runs long.

The stations. Each one gets a card: what it is, what it needs on the table, who runs it, and how long it takes. The Grand Tour needs a machine from each season out of its box and working before anybody arrives. The grader station needs the laptop, the account already logged in, and the verdict screen where the room can see it. Your authored problem needs the story printed, the input format printed, and your test data somewhere the hunters cannot get at it.

The jobs. Everybody present gets one, written on the board with their name beside it, including the youngest person in the house, whose job is not a decoration. Somebody holds the timer for the Talk. Somebody keeps the water going. Somebody starts and stops the recording. A guest with no job stands around, and standing around is how a guest starts checking their phone.

The invitations, and this is the part that makes it real. Write them, and send them this week rather than mentioning it to people. Each one carries the date, the start time, where it is, roughly how long it runs, and one honest sentence about what they are coming to see. If you want somebody to say yes, they have to be asked in advance and in writing.

One design rule, and it is the difference between a plan and a wish. Build it so it runs with whoever actually turns up. If the room is four people, it runs. If somebody joins on a call, they get a job too and somebody has to point the camera at the right thing at the right moment. Write the version that survives a missing guest, because a programme that only works at full strength is a programme that is already going wrong.
checklist: The run of show is on the board in order, with a clock time and a length beside every segment, and two deliberate gaps in it
Every station has a card saying what it needs, who runs it and how long it takes
Every person expected has a written job, including my Sprout, and no job is a decoration
The invitations are written and actually sent, with the date, the start time, the place and one honest sentence about what it is
I said out loud how the morning runs if somebody cannot come, and the board says so too

figure.alt: A command travelling from Earth to Mars and a reply travelling back, each leg taking somewhere between about 3 and 22 minutes at the speed of light depending on how far apart the planets are that day. Because a joystick needs feedback in a fraction of a second to feel usable, engineers send a whole day's plan of moves at once instead of steering the rover live.

items.s: no live joystick: a day's plan sent at once

steps.title: Why nobody drives a Mars rover live
steps.body:
Every command sent to a Mars rover travels as radio. Radio moves at light speed, about 300,000 kilometres a second, the fastest anything can travel.

That still is not fast enough to feel instant. Earth and Mars are never a fixed distance apart, since both planets orbit the sun at different paces. The distance ranges from about 54.6 million kilometres at their closest to about 401 million kilometres at their farthest. At those distances, a one-way radio signal takes somewhere between about 3 and 22 minutes to arrive. The same delay applies to the reply coming back.

A joystick needs feedback in a fraction of a second to feel usable, so nobody steers a rover like a remote-control car. Engineers on Earth send a whole day's plan of moves at once. The rover checks its own sensors, follows the plan itself, then reports back what actually happened, minutes later.

Your own free build ran on the opposite plan: you were right there, testing and fixing in real time, something a rover never gets.

steps.title: Card version two, prove the tools, pack the kit
steps.body:
Three jobs, all of them cheaper today than at dawn on Saturday.

Version two of the card. Get out the card as you revised it at the oasis, and put the route page and the pace chart beside it. Now change only what the evidence tells you to change. A line survives if the crossing gave you no reason to touch it. A line changes if the chart says something you did not expect, and the change has to name the thing on the chart it came from. Nothing goes on the card because it sounds wise. Write version two at the top, and keep version one, because the two of them side by side are a record of how your own thinking moved and you will want that in week 12.

Prove the tools, and start by logging in, because this is the part that surprises people. Open a past problem page while you are logged out and read the box under the problem: it says the contest has ended and no further submissions are allowed, and there is nowhere to submit anything. Now log in and look at the same page again. Logged in, the site lets you send solutions to problems from contests that finished years ago and hands them to the same judging server, which the site calls analysis mode. So the account is not a detail, it is the whole door. Then submit a solution you already own, say out loud what verdict you expect before you press the button, and compare.

Check the two facts about your chosen contest without spoiling it. Do not open any of its problems. Write down its date, and from the date write the input shape: contests before the December 2020 one name a file in the INPUT FORMAT heading, and your program has to open exactly that file and write exactly the matching output file, while from the December 2020 contest onward the heading names the terminal instead and you read standard input and print the answer. Then write the window. The contest instructions say contests are typically four to five contiguous hours, and the length belongs to the contest rather than to Bronze, so look up which one you picked and write its hours down. Both facts go on the back of the card. On the morning, the problem page in front of you is the final authority, not this page, not the card, and not your memory.

Decide the after, now. When the clock stops on Saturday you may, if you want it, take one problem again in C++, untimed, with nothing riding on it. That is genuinely optional and nobody is disappointed either way. Decide today whether you want it and roughly which problem you would pick, and write it on the back of the card, because somebody at the end of a long morning should not be asked to decide about doing more work.

Then set the kit out where it will sit: card, clock, blank paper, pencil, water. No phone on the desk.
checklist: Version two of the card exists, version one is still readable, and every change names the thing on the pace chart it came from
I looked at a past problem page logged out and then logged in, and I can say what changes
I submitted a solution I already own, after saying out loud what verdict I expected
The contest date, its input shape and its window length are on the back of the card, and I opened none of its problems
The kit is out, the phone is not, and I have written down what I want to do after the clock stops

steps.title: Saturday: the third crossing
steps.body:
The date is on the wall map under the third sun, in your handwriting, because you chose it. That is all the map says about it and all it is ever going to say.

What it is. One complete past Bronze contest from the archive, the one you picked. The whole window that contest ran for. Python. Alone, at the dawn you named, breaks at your call, a proctor at the door with the same job description as last time: they do not read the problems, they do not answer a question about one, and they do not make a face at your screen. One thing is on the desk that was not there in week 7, and it is your own card.

The clock is still yours. The site does not run a timer on a contest that ended years ago, so you write the start time at the top of the route page, start the analog clock, and stop when your window is up even if you are mid-sentence.

The route page again, all morning, times written in the margin as things happen. Started reading. Opened the editor. Submitted. Rejected, back to the paper. Stood up. Those times are the morning's only real data, and they do not exist unless you write them at the time.

Two true things about the grader, both worth knowing before you sit down. Resubmitting carries no penalty, and the site's own instructions ask you to be reasonable about the rate so you are not hammering their server. And in a live contest, which is what December is, only the last solution you submit for a problem gets graded, which is a rule you want in your hands long before it matters.

Then the pace, and this part is yours and nobody else's. Afterwards, put this morning's pace page next to week 7's and look at the difference. Then explain it, and explain it honestly, which means the job is to lay the candidates out rather than to announce a cause. It was a different contest with different problems. You slept differently. You had a card this time. You had done this once before. Some of those push one way, some push the other, and one pair of mornings cannot separate them. Naming the honest candidates and saying which ones you cannot tell apart is a better answer than picking the flattering one, and it is the same discipline you use on a program that looks right.

And after the clock has stopped, only if you want it: one problem, again, in C++, untimed, nothing riding on it, using only tools you already have. If it goes nowhere, that is a fine outcome and it goes in the ledger exactly as it happened.

The debrief is the next day, not the same day. Route and weather, one pack item, the week 3 form, no score anywhere in it. How many the grader accepted is not the report.

steps.title: The bug diary: predict the morning before you have it
steps.body:
Almost no code this week, so the diary gets the entry that only works if you write it before you know the answer.

Before Saturday, on one page: your predicted minutes on each of the three problems, and your predicted total. Then the two extras that make it interesting. Which problem do you expect to be the one you park, and at roughly what time on the clock do you expect the morning to turn, meaning the moment when you can feel that its shape is decided.

Fold the page over. Do not look at it during the morning, because a prediction you can see turns into an instruction.

On Sunday, open it beside the route page and mark the gaps. Not to score the prediction, which is not the point, but to find out which direction you are wrong in. Almost everybody is wrong in a consistent direction, and knowing your own direction is worth more than being right, because it is the thing you can correct for in October.

That is the mirage in its home clothes. Feeling fast and being fast are two different states, they feel identical from the inside, and a page written in advance is one of the very few things that can tell them apart.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A photo of the finished dossier board with the run of show, the station cards and the job list readable. A photo of one invitation as it was sent. Then the two cards side by side, version one and version two, close enough to read every line. Then the verdict screen from the dry run with your written prediction beside it. Then, after Sunday, the route page with the clock times in the margin, the two pace pages side by side, and the debrief in the week 3 form. If you took a problem again in C++ after the clock stopped, add the code and whatever the grader said about it, accepted or not.
